questions.problem:
Consider the system of linear equations given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+2y=-11 \\ y+7x=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that the system has exactly one solution, which of the following statements are true?

- The coefficient matrix is not invertible
- The determinant of the coefficient matrix is not zero
- The lines $x+2y=-11$ and $y+7x=4$ intersect at infinitely many  points
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

Also, we are told that the second part of the invertible matrix theorem is true. So, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement I is false by the first part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement II is true. According to the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem, the determinant cannot be $0.$

- Statement III is false by the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, only statement II is true.

questions.problem:
Let $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ -5 & k\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ where $k$ is a constant such that $k\ne 1.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $det(A)\ne 0$
- $Ax=0$ has no solution
- The lines $5x-y=-1$ and $-5x+ky=0$ intersect exactly at one point
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ -5 & k\end{aligned}] \\  & =5\cdot k-(-1)\cdot (-5) \\  & =5k-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $5k-5\ne 0$ if $k\ne 1.$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is false. According to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, there must be a unique zero solution to $Ax=0.$

- Statement III is true. According to the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem, the lines must intersect at exactly one point.

Finally, only statements I and III are true.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

According to the invertible matrix theorem, if the lines $x+y=3$ and $x-ky=1$  intersect at exactly one point, then 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -k\end{aligned}]
$$

is invertible and $det(A)\ne 0.$ 
Additionally, the unique solution to $Ax=0$ is $⟨0,0⟩$ and

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -k\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

has exactly one solution, which is the intersection point of the lines.

Finally, notice that if $k$ can't be equal to $-1,$ since  $det[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -(-1)\end{aligned}]=0.$

Therefore, the true statement is as follows:

*f the lines intersect at exactly one point, then $det[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -k\end{aligned}]\ne 0.$*

Example: 
                    Identifying a True Statement Given a 2x2 Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14116902/assets/2de33a648364672e24ed14d9ceb606eeec07da3dc5e8ab1bdf4c00440f2229ac.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14116902/assets/b3ca8db3f26fed706e2786f2c7a09b39800bb249f72565039d7fe6493a813507.svg) where $k\neq 4$ is a constant. Which of the following statements are true?

- $\det(A) = 0$

- $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has no solutions

- The lines $x-2y=1$ and $-2x+ky=-3$ intersect at exactly one point
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that given ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14116902/assets/3a82d0f5d2e89d80c3e5f541e205d3052264d967db9736d86de3f52418319a29.svg), then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution for any $2 \times 1$ column vector $\mathbf{b}.$

- The system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines $a_{11}x+a_{12}y=b_1$ and $a_{21}x+a_{22}y=b_2$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $\det(A) \neq 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is false. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & k\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot k-(-2)\cdot (-2) \\  & =k-4,\end{aligned}
$$

where $k - 4 \neq 0$ if $k \neq 4.$ 

So, since the fifth part in the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is false. According to the second part of the invertible matrix theorem, there must be exactly one solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$

- Statement III is true by the fourth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, only statement III is true.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Completing a True Statement
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following completes the statement so that it is true:

*If a $2\times2$-matrix $A$ is invertible, then $\text{__________}$ . *

- $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has infinitely many solutions

- $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has exactly one solution

- $\det(A) = 0$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that given ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14116902/assets/60966175c795cda23b462c4dc57bb694acbd0ec5ce3ffda29cb20fba41a86d60.svg), then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution for any $2 \times 1$ column vector $\mathbf{b}.$

- The system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines $a_{11}x+a_{12}y=b_1$ and $a_{21}x+a_{22}y=b_2$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $\det(A) \neq 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

Notice that since the first part of the invertible matrix theorem is true ($A$ is invertible), all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem, only option II gives us a true statement:

- *If $A$ is invertible, then $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has exactly one solution.* $\quad \color{green}\checkmark$

tutorials.problem:
Consider a system of two linear equations with two variables 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and let
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14116902/assets/73c4f1122f53beb4bea2619922226e641d7ac1dd2bb611106d8a33dc13a7abbd.svg)

Recall that we can write the system as $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.$ The **invertible matrix theorem** says the following statements are equivalent:

- $A$ is invertible (that is, $A^{-1}$ exists).

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Consider a system of two linear equations with two variables 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1} \\ {a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and let
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14116902/assets/73c4f1122f53beb4bea2619922226e641d7ac1dd2bb611106d8a33dc13a7abbd.svg)

Recall that we can write the system as $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.$ The **invertible matrix theorem** says the following statements are equivalent:

- $A$ is invertible (that is, $A^{-1}$ exists).

- The system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution for any $2 \times 1$ column vector $\mathbf{b}$ (we call such systems consistent independent).

- The system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has the unique solution ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14116902/assets/9f196772fa8ca5829a00c8f4378f2a51f423cf6e27fdc8470e245be0c4005f2c.svg)

- The lines ${\color{red}{a_{11}}}x+{\color{red}{a_{12}}}y={\color{blue}{b_1}}$ and ${\color{red}{a_{21}}}x+{\color{red}{a_{22}}}y={\color{blue}{b_2}}$ intersect at one point.

- The  determinant of $A$ is nonzero (that is, $\det(A) \neq 0$).
